## Diagnostic Activity

Answer the following questions from memory before reading further.

1. Compute the simple interest earned on €1,000 invested at 5% per year
   for 2 years.
2. Is compound interest modelled by an arithmetic or geometric sequence?
3. A monthly interest rate is 0.5%. What is the equivalent annual rate
   under simple (proportional) conversion?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Check your answers

1. $1{,}000 \times 0.05 \times 2 = €100.$
2. Geometric — each period multiplies the capital by a constant factor
   $(1+i).$
3. $0.5\% \times 12 = 6\%$ per year.
:::

Use your results to identify topics needing attention.

## Opening Problem

You invest €5,000 at an annual rate of 4%. Bank A compounds the
interest once a year; Bank B compounds it every month (same annual
rate).

> After 10 years, how much more does Bank B give you than Bank A?
> Is the difference significant?

Write down your estimate before continuing.

## Core Concepts

Simple interest and compound interest are two different ways of
computing, for example, the return on invested capital or the cost of a
loan. Each has its practical uses depending on the financial and economic
context. They are the direct application of the arithmetic and geometric
sequences studied in Module 4.

### Simple Interest

::: {.callout-note}
#### Principle
With **simple interest**, interest is computed only on the **initial**
capital, without reinvestment. The interest is the same for each period,
so the acquired capital follows an **arithmetic** sequence.
:::

Let $C_0$ be the initial capital, $i$ the interest rate per period, and
$n$ the number of periods. The interest of one period is $C_0\,i$
(constant), so:

$$
\text{Interest over } n \text{ periods} = C_0\,i\,n,
\qquad
C_n = C_0\,(1 + i\,n).
$$

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Typical uses of simple interest
- short-term loans;
- one-off investments without reinvestment;
- late-payment penalties and fees.
:::

#### Worked example

We invest $100{,}000$ € at a simple annual rate of $4\%$ for $4$ years.
The yearly interest is constant: $100{,}000 \times 0.04 = 4{,}000$ € per
year. After $4$ years the acquired capital is

$$
C_4 = 100{,}000\,(1 + 0.04 \times 4) = 100{,}000 \times 1.16
    = 116{,}000 \text{ €}.
$$

### Converting Interest Rates

Sometimes the rate and the period are not expressed in the same unit of
time. Under the **simple** (proportional) convention, we scale the rate
proportionally to the period.

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Proportional conversion (simple regime)
An annual rate $i_{\text{year}}$ corresponds to a monthly rate
$i_{\text{month}} = \dfrac{i_{\text{year}}}{12}$, and conversely
$i_{\text{year}} = 12\,i_{\text{month}}$.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Rate exercises (click for solutions)
1. Convert an annual rate of $6\%$ to a monthly rate:
   $\dfrac{6\%}{12} = 0.5\%$ per month.
2. Convert a monthly rate of $1\%$ to an annual rate:
   $12 \times 1\% = 12\%$ per year.
3. A capital of $5{,}000$ € invested for $4$ months earns $50$ € of
   interest. Find the annual rate. The $4$-month rate is
   $\dfrac{50}{5000} = 1\%$, so the monthly rate is $0.25\%$ and the
   annual rate is $12 \times 0.25\% = 3\%$.
:::

### Compound Interest

::: {.callout-note}
#### Principle
With **compound interest**, the interest earned each period is added to
the capital and itself earns interest in the following periods (the
"snowball" effect). The acquired capital follows a **geometric**
sequence.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Derivation — the compound-interest formula (click to expand)
At the end of one period the capital is multiplied by $(1 + i)$: the
capital $C_0$ becomes $C_1 = C_0 + C_0 i = C_0(1 + i)$. Repeating,
$C_2 = C_1(1 + i) = C_0(1 + i)^2$, and by induction

$$
C_n = C_0\,(1 + i)^{\,n}.
$$

This is exactly a geometric sequence with first term $C_0$ and common
ratio $q = 1 + i$. The interest earned over $n$ periods is
$C_n - C_0 = C_0\big[(1 + i)^n - 1\big]$.
:::

#### Worked example

We invest $100{,}000$ € at a compound annual rate of $5\%$ for $10$
years:

$$
C_{10} = 100{,}000 \times 1.05^{10} \approx 162{,}889 \text{ €}.
$$

For comparison, the **same** capital at a **simple** rate of $6\%$ for
$10$ years gives $100{,}000(1 + 0.06 \times 10) = 160{,}000$ €: over a
long horizon the compounding effect can outweigh a higher simple rate —
but not always, as the final-exam case in Module 8 shows.

::: {.callout-important}
#### Exam tip — equivalent compound rate
Converting a compound rate between periods is **not** proportional. A
monthly compound rate $i_m$ corresponds to the annual rate
$i_{\text{year}} = (1 + i_m)^{12} - 1$. For $i_m = 0.5\%$ this gives
$(1.005)^{12} - 1 \approx 6.17\%$, not $6\%$.
:::

### Average Placement Rate

The **average placement rate** is the single rate that would produce the
same final result (the same acquired capital) as a set of distinct
investments, each with its own rate, amount, and duration. It summarises
the overall performance of several combined investments in one figure.

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Present value

$$P = \frac{V_c}{(1 + i)^n}$$

The present value $P$ is the initial capital that would produce a future
value $V_c$ at rate $i$ after $n$ periods — it lets us compare cash
flows at different points in time.
:::

## Worked Example

### Worked example — Bank A vs Bank B (the Opening Problem)

We now solve the problem posed in §2 step by step.

**Bank A** — annual compounding ($k = 1$):

$$
V_A = 5{,}000 \times (1 + 0.04)^{10}
    = 5{,}000 \times 1.04^{10}
    \approx 7{,}401.22 \text{ €}.
$$

**Bank B** — monthly compounding ($k = 12$):

$$
V_B = 5{,}000 \times \!\left(1 + \frac{0.04}{12}\right)^{10 \times 12}
    = 5{,}000 \times (1.003\overline{3})^{120}
    \approx 7{,}453.71 \text{ €}.
$$

**Difference**:

$$
7{,}453.71 - 7{,}401.22 = 52.49 \text{ €}.
$$

Monthly compounding yields €52.49 more — a modest but real gain from
the compounding frequency.

## Guided Practice

An employee places €3,000 in a savings account offering a compound
annual rate of 3.5%, compounded quarterly.

1. Write the formula for the acquired capital after $n$ years.
2. Calculate the acquired capital after 4 years.
3. How many years does it take to double the initial capital?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### Hint
With quarterly compounding, $k = 4$. Use
$V_c = P\!\left(1 + \dfrac{i}{k}\right)^{nk}$ with $P = 3{,}000$,
$i = 0.035$, $k = 4$. For doubling, solve
$\left(1 + \dfrac{0.035}{4}\right)^{4n} = 2$.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Show the solution

**1. Formula:**

$$
V_c = 3{,}000 \times \!\left(1 + \frac{0.035}{4}\right)^{4n}
    = 3{,}000 \times 1.00875^{4n}.
$$

**2. After 4 years** ($n = 4$, so the exponent is $4 \times 4 = 16$):

$$
V_c = 3{,}000 \times 1.00875^{16}
    \approx 3{,}000 \times 1.1490
    \approx 3{,}447 \text{ €}.
$$

**3. Doubling:** solve $(1.00875)^{4n} = 2$. Testing $n = 20$:
$(1.00875)^{80} \approx 2.002 \approx 2$. About **20 years**.
:::

## Interactive Exploration

Use the controls below to explore how the principal, rate, number of
years, and compounding frequency interact.

```{ojs}
viewof principal = Inputs.range([100, 10000], {
  value: 5000,
  step: 100,
  label: "Principal P (€)"
})

viewof rate = Inputs.range([0, 20], {
  value: 4,
  step: 0.1,
  label: "Annual rate i (%)"
})

viewof periods = Inputs.range([1, 30], {
  value: 10,
  step: 1,
  label: "Number of years n"
})

viewof freq = Inputs.select([1, 2, 4, 12], {
  value: 1,
  label: "Capitalisation frequency k (per year)"
})
```

```{ojs}
i = rate / 100
simpleVal = principal * (1 + i * periods)
compoundVal = principal * Math.pow(1 + i / freq, periods * freq)
cumInterest = compoundVal - principal

timeData = Array.from({length: periods + 1}, (_, t) => ({
  t,
  compound: principal * Math.pow(1 + i / freq, t * freq),
  simple: principal * (1 + i * t)
}))

growthChart = Plot.plot({
  marks: [
    Plot.line(timeData, {x: "t", y: "compound", stroke: "steelblue",
      label: "Compound"}),
    Plot.line(timeData, {x: "t", y: "simple", stroke: "orange",
      strokeDash: [4, 4], label: "Simple"}),
    Plot.dot(timeData, {x: "t", y: "compound", fill: "steelblue", r: 3}),
    Plot.dot(timeData, {x: "t", y: "simple", fill: "orange", r: 3})
  ],
  x: {label: "Year"},
  y: {label: "Capital (€)"},
  color: {legend: true}
})
```

```{ojs}
html`
<div style="margin-bottom:1rem">${growthChart}</div>
<div class="metric-grid">
  <div class="metric-card">
    <span class="metric-label">Simple interest value</span>
    <strong>${simpleVal.toFixed(2)} €</strong>
  </div>
  <div class="metric-card">
    <span class="metric-label">Compound interest value</span>
    <strong>${compoundVal.toFixed(2)} €</strong>
  </div>
  <div class="metric-card">
    <span class="metric-label">Cumulative interest earned</span>
    <strong>${cumInterest.toFixed(2)} €</strong>
  </div>
  <div class="metric-card">
    <span class="metric-label">Gain over simple interest</span>
    <strong>${(compoundVal - simpleVal).toFixed(2)} €</strong>
  </div>
</div>
`
```

### Investigation

1. Set $k = 1$ (annual). Now set $k = 12$ (monthly), keeping all other
   parameters fixed. How much extra does monthly compounding earn after
   10 years?
2. Keep $k = 1$ and increase $n$ from 5 to 30. Does the gap between
   compound and simple interest grow slowly or quickly?
3. Which has more impact on the final compound value: doubling the rate
   or doubling the number of years? Test with the sliders.
4. Set $i = 0$ (zero rate). What do both formulas give? Why?

## Applied Problem

A firm needs to repay a loan of €200,000 in 8 years. Two banks compete
for the business. **Bank A** offers a simple annual rate of 7%. **Bank B**
offers a compound annual rate of 5.5%.

1. Calculate the total amount repaid to each bank after 8 years.
2. Which bank offers the better deal?
3. Bank A also offers to apply its rate monthly under simple
   (proportional) conversion. What is the monthly rate? What is the
   total repayment?
4. Bank B offers monthly compounding at the same annual rate. What is
   the effective annual compound rate? Is it higher or lower than 5.5%?

## Common Errors

::: {.callout-warning}
#### Common error — applying proportional conversion to compound rates

A student converts a monthly compound rate of 0.5% to an annual rate as
$0.5\% \times 12 = 6\%$.

This is only valid for **simple** (proportional) rates. For **compound**
rates, the correct conversion is:

$$
i_{\text{year}} = (1 + i_{\text{month}})^{12} - 1
               = (1.005)^{12} - 1
               \approx 6.17\%.
$$

Always use the compound-rate conversion formula when interest is
reinvested each period.
:::

## Check Your Understanding

1. €8,000 invested at 3% simple interest for 5 years. What is the
   acquired capital?
2. What does it mean economically when the capitalisation frequency $k$
   increases while the annual rate stays fixed?
3. €10,000 invested at 4% compound (annual) for 8 years. Calculate the
   acquired capital.
4. A student computes the annual compound rate equivalent to a monthly
   rate of 1% as $1\% \times 12 = 12\%$. What is the correct answer?
5. Which repayment is smaller: €100,000 at 6% simple for 10 years, or
   €100,000 at 5% compound for 10 years?

## Summary

1. Simple interest applies the rate to the original capital only
   ($V_s = P(1+in)$); compound interest applies it to the growing
   capital ($V_c = P(1+i/k)^{nk}$) — the difference grows with time
   and rate.
2. Simple interest rates convert proportionally across periods; compound
   rates do not — converting $i_m$ to an annual rate requires
   $(1+i_m)^{12} - 1$, which always gives a higher annual rate.
3. The capitalisation frequency $k$ matters: more frequent compounding
   (quarterly, monthly, daily) produces a higher final value for the
   same nominal annual rate, because interest starts earning interest
   sooner.
